Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The people responsible have faced no consequences
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body Shame' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a civilian-in-war-zone trauma unless there is some indication of bodily violation, injury, or humiliation. The other selected items center on injustice, impunity, hypervigilance, dissociative/fragmented memory, and avoidance, but provide no supporting context for body-focused shame, making this item stand out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The Threat items emphasize pervasive current danger and hypervigilance (scanning exits, needing to stay alert at night), but the formulation specifically has Triggers → Threat inactive. In this profile, Triggers are concrete reminders such as car sounds and related media, yet the Threat items are generalized and not plausibly linked to those triggers; this makes the threat presentation feel disconnected from the trigger pattern.

vignette: Rajesh Kumar, a 74‑year‑old welder in a small steel‑making plant on the outskirts of Philadelphia, first came to notice himself only when the world of steel hissed and clanged too loudly for his own mind. Seventy years ago, in a war‑torn region of his native South East Asia, he had been caught in a shelling that left a scorched patch of earth in his memory and a deep scar on his chest. The explosion had broken a machine, sending shrapnel flying, and the sudden roar of the blast had been swallowed by the thundering of the surrounding artillery. From that night onward, the mere rumble of a passing truck or the distant clatter of a factory overhead could summon the memory of that night in a flash of darkness. The echo of that sound has become a trigger that is impossible to ignore. When Rajesh hears the screech of a car horn or the metallic clang of a construction crane, he automatically retreats into a silence that feels safer. He avoids talking about the war, even with his wife, because the conversation forces him to relive the night and the terror of the explosion. Whenever the memory intrudes, he thinks of something else—a picture of his daughter’s graduation, a recipe he’s never tried—to redirect his mind. In the open workshop, where the beams rise high and the air is thin, he refuses to walk across the floor, preferring the safety of closed corners. These maladaptive strategies are the first defense that the car sounds, the low buzz of exhaust, and the brief images from television news that replay the war scene, set into motion a chain that blocks the flow of his thoughts and emotions. The triggers do more than just bring back fragments of the event; they also sharpen the sense that the memory is incomplete, that the full picture of that night has slipped through his fingers. The weight of injustice, that nothing had been done for him after the war, makes the triggers feel even more oppressive. Rajesh believes that the war’s aftermath has been unfair, that the authorities did nothing to compensate the survivors, and that the responsibility lies solely with the perpetrators. These convictions propel him to avoid speaking further, to keep his voice low, and to avoid any place that reminds him of open spaces. The sense of unfairness heightens his hypervigilance: he finds it difficult to concentrate on welding the pipe, and his mind constantly darts to the possibility of another blast. The relentless need to stay alert keeps him from falling asleep; he wakes up with his heart racing, convinced the sound of a distant train is another reminder of the war. In the darkness of his bedroom, his mind turns to the injustice he feels, and the belief only feeds back into the cycle of avoidance and threat. Rajesh’s memory of the night is fractured; he can only recall isolated bursts— the heat, the sudden crack of the shell, a splash of blood. He feels that the memory is not truly his; it belongs to someone else, a story that was forced onto him. Because it feels unreal, he questions its truth. This alien feeling of the memory pushes him to pull back even more, avoiding any discussion that might force him to reconstruct the narrative. It also amplifies his sense of injustice, because he is convinced that the only version of the story he remembers is a false version that he must not trust. Every time a trigger surfaces—a honking car, a brief flash of a war documentary on his television—his mind leaps to the incomplete picture, reinforcing the feeling that his experience was unjust and that he is the only one left with a distorted, untrustworthy version. The triggers, the memory, and the appraisal of injustice feed into one another, creating a closed loop that pulls him further into avoidance. The hypervigilance that Rajesh feels is not only a reaction to the triggers; it is the very mechanism that makes the triggers so persistent. He is constantly scanning the air for the next whir of a motor or the faint crackle of static, and each new sound becomes a potential reminder of that night. This constant scanning, a threat that keeps him on guard, magnifies every cue in the environment and makes the triggers unavoidable. The more he scans, the more he hears, and the more he hears, the more he feels threatened. Avoidance becomes the only way Rajesh can preserve the fragmentary memory he has left. By shunning conversations and refusing to step into open spaces, he preserves the integrity of his incomplete recollection. Yet the avoidance itself creates new memories of loss— the time he missed his son’s birthday because he stayed home to rest, the opportunity he lost to ask his colleagues about the quality of a weld. These new memories add to his sense that the war and its aftereffects were unjust and that he has no control over the present or the future. The more he avoids, the more he feels responsible for the damage to his life. His self‑blame grows, as if the very act of living in a world of steel and sparks is a testament that he failed to protect himself or his community. Rajesh’s decision to seek help has come after a series of nights in which he could not sleep, waking each morning with his chest tight and his mind racing through the war’s images. He feared that the endless cycle of avoidance, hypervigilance, and fragmented memory would eventually erode his sense of self and destroy the small joys he still clings to—his wife’s hand in his, the steady hiss of the welding arc, the quiet hum of the plant at night. What keeps him most afraid is the idea that he might lose the last remaining connection to a life he once knew, and what he hopes for is to reclaim the ability to breathe freely, to speak without fear, and to feel the peace that he has not known since that night.
